**Inventory**

A thousand words is a strange sum. Enough for a short story if the story is spare, enough for an argument if the argument is small. Too many for a lie, too few for a life. When someone hands you a number like that, the first temptation is to spend it on the number itself — to write about the writing, to circle the plate without swinging. I feel that pull. I'm resisting it, mostly. Consider this paragraph a tax.

Here is what I want to do instead: make a list of things I think are worth keeping. Not important things. The other kind.

The sound a hardcover makes when you close it too fast — that soft pneumatic thud, the little exhale of trapped air. Book-breath. Paperbacks don't do it. It requires a certain rigidity of spine, a willingness to hold shape.

The moment in a conversation when both people stop performing. You can hear it happen. The sentences get shorter and worse. Someone says "yeah, no, I don't know" and means something enormous by it. I think most of what passes between people passes in exactly those degraded sentences, the ones that would look like nothing on a transcript.

Second sleep. The forty minutes after the alarm and before the surrender, which is the only sleep that feels like a possession rather than a duty.

The way certain words carry the smell of the decade they were coined in. *Groovy.* *Yuppie.* *Blog.* You cannot say them neutrally; they arrive wearing clothes.

Dogs at the moment they decide to lie down — the collapse, the total abdication of vertebrae. No animal has ever committed to anything as fully as a dog commits to the floor.

The particular guilt of a plant you have not watered. It isn't a big guilt. It sits somewhere in the middle range of the moral instrument, and yet it recurs, it accumulates, it has a way of standing in for every larger neglect. I suspect houseplants are the cheapest available mirror.

Rain starting while you're already outside and have already accepted that you'll be wet. There is a threshold past which weather stops being an obstacle and becomes a fact, and crossing it is one of the few reliable pleasures available in public.

The first cold snap of autumn, when the air acquires an edge and everyone becomes briefly, stupidly hopeful, as though the year were starting over instead of ending. September is the real New Year and always has been. January is an administrative fiction.

Handwriting on an envelope you weren't expecting. Even now. Even from institutions.

The fact that most people, if you ask them what they were doing at 3 p.m. on a random Tuesday four years ago, will not only fail to answer but will find the failure unremarkable. Nearly all of our hours are like this. We are, statistically, made almost entirely of forgotten afternoons. I don't find this sad, exactly. It seems more like the way sediment works. The forgetting is what makes the pressure that makes the stone.

Overheard fragments. "—and that's when I found out she'd been a nun." "—but the dog knew." "—he doesn't believe in Tuesdays, which, honestly, respect." Every one of these is the middle of something. The city is full of middles, and you are never given the ends, and this is fine; the middle is where the information is.

The way a stranger will hold a door for slightly too long, so that you have to break into a small apologetic trot, and both of you have now been mildly inconvenienced by kindness, and neither of you would trade it.

The competence of people at their jobs. A butcher's economy of motion. A nurse finding a vein on the first try. The guy at the hardware store who listens to your incoherent description of a bracket for eleven seconds and then walks, without hesitation, to aisle six. I think this is close to the most beautiful thing humans do, and it goes almost entirely unpraised because it looks like nothing. Mastery's whole signature is looking like nothing.

Lemons. Not as flavor — as objects. The waxy, dimpled, faintly absurd solidity of them. If you had never seen one and someone described it, you would not believe the color.

Being wrong in public and surviving it. The specific lightness afterward, like setting down a heavy bag you'd forgotten you were carrying, having spent all that energy on a defense of a position you didn't even like.

The last four pages of a good novel, read slower and slower, the way you'd walk the last stretch home in weather you liked.

Snow at night, in a streetlight, seen from a window, by someone who does not have to go anywhere.

And the thing about a list like this — I'm at about seven hundred words, I can feel the floor coming — is that it's a bluff. It pretends to be a catalogue of the world when it's really a self-portrait. Tell me what you'd save and I'll tell you where you've been standing. My list has no children in it, no injuries, no music. Someone else's would be all three. The gaps are the actual content. Every inventory is a confession about what the inventory-taker had access to.

Which is maybe the only thing I actually know: that attention is not neutral, that noticing is a kind of authorship, and that anyone who tells you they're simply describing the world has quietly done a great deal of choosing on your behalf. Including me. Including now.

So I'll end with the honest version. A thousand words is not much. But it is more than most moments get. The overwhelming majority of what happens goes unrecorded, unpraised, unremembered — the forgotten afternoons, the sediment. To spend a thousand words on book-breath and lemons is not frivolous. It's a small correction to an enormous imbalance, and the imbalance will win, and the correction is still worth making.

The hardcover closes. The air goes out with that sound.

Yeah, no. I don't know.

But I think that's what I wanted to say.
